papers.title_in_file: An Introduction to the Syntax and Content of Cyc
papers.what_it_is: A 2006 Cycorp overview of the CycL language and the OpenCyc and ResearchCyc ontologies, with example assertions.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Cyc project has spent the past twenty years, approximately 900 person-years of effort, building a knowledge base intended to capture a broad selection of common-sense background knowledge.
quotes: The Cyc project has spent the past twenty years— approximately 900 person-years of effort—building a knowledge base that is intended to capture a broad selection of common-sense background knowledge.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Cyc KB contains more than 2.2 million assertions describing more than 250,000 terms, including nearly 15,000 predicates.
quotes: The Cyc KB contains more than 2.2 million assertions (facts and rules) describing more than 250,000 terms, including nearly 15,000 predicates.
assertions.reader_inference: A 2006 snapshot; the paper gives no method for the count.

assertions.value: The authors state that the current version of OpenCyc includes an ontology of 47,000 terms, defined and elaborated using 306,000 assertions, and that this is a small subset of the total content of Cyc.
quotes: In its current version, OpenCyc includes an ontology of 47,000 terms, which are defined and elaborated using 306,000 assertions.

assertions.value: The authors state the thesis underlying Cyc: special-purpose domain systems can be brittle and difficult to extend to new or unforeseen problems.
quotes: these systems can be brittle [Friedland et al 2004] and difficult to extend to new or unforeseen problems or problem areas [Lenat 1995]
assertions.reader_inference: The brittleness claim is attributed to Friedland et al 2004 and Lenat 1995, not shown here.

assertions.value: The authors state that a primary goal of the Cyc project has been to build a large knowledge base of formalized background knowledge suitable for reasoning in a variety of domains.
quotes: a primary goal of the Cyc project has been to build a large knowledge base containing a store of formalized background knowledge suitable for supporting reasoning in a variety of domains
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the project goal in the abstract.

assertions.value: The authors state that CycL's syntax expresses a number of extensions to first order logic, including a quoting mechanism that separates knowledge about a concept from knowledge about the term that denotes it.
quotes: CycL’s syntax expresses a number of extensions to first order-logic
It includes a quoting mechanism to enable differentiation between knowledge involving a concept, as opposed to knowledge about the term that expresses the concept.

assertions.value: The authors state that CycL has features of higher-order logics: quantification over predicates, functions and sentences, and predicates that take predicates as values, in some cases including themselves.
quotes: there is quantification over predicates, functions, and sentences,
and there is the ability for predicates to take predicates as values, including themselves in some cases.

assertions.value: The authors give an example of quoting: the ontology can hold that all dogs are mammals and also facts about the term #$Dog, such as when it was created and by whom.
quotes: such as when it was created and by whom

assertions.value: The authors state that quoting and higher-order extensions let the semantics of the language's terms be represented in the same language as all other knowledge, so that all knowledge has a common representational basis and is mutually accessible to inference.
quotes: so that all knowledge has a common representational basis and is mutually accessible to inference

assertions.value: The authors state that the higher-order features allow rule macro predicates, which give compact expressions of relationships that would otherwise require rules.
quotes: which allow for compact expressions of relationships that would otherwise require rules

assertions.value: The authors state that OpenCyc is a taxonomic projection of the Cyc Knowledge Base that primarily describes Cyc's taxonomic and definitional ontology, with class membership and subsumption expressed by isa and genls.
quotes: OpenCyc is, at heart, a taxonomic projection of the Cyc Knowledge Base
expressed with the predicates isa and genls, respectively
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state what OpenCyc covers.

assertions.value: The authors state that a subsumption relationship exists among predicates, where the holding of one relation to some arguments implies the holding of another relation to those arguments, expressed via genlPreds.
quotes: where the holding of one relation to some set of arguments implies the holding of another relationship to those arguments (expressed via genlPreds)
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define genlPreds here.

assertions.value: The authors define a CycL sentence that conforms to the grammar but not to its semantic requirements as semantically ill-formed, and state that semantic well-formedness implements constraints on common-sense use of relationships and helps automate validation by rejecting the formal equivalents of ridiculous sentences.
quotes: If a CycL sentence conforms to the grammar but not its semantic requirements, it is said to be semantically ill-formed.
helps automate the validation of knowledge, by rejecting the formal equivalents of ridiculous sentences
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the term in the text.

assertions.value: The authors give the example sentence 'Julia gave birth to a prime number' as grammatically well-formed but expressing a confused idea that could not be true in any context.
quotes: Julia gave birth to a prime number.
it expresses a confused idea that could not be true in any context
assertions.certainty_reason: Footnote 1 gives this as the authors' illustration.

assertions.value: The authors define the argument constraint as knowledge of what types of entities can be the values of a predicate or function, and give biologicalMother with the assertions isa IrreflexiveBinaryPredicate, arg1Isa Animal and arg2Isa FemaleAnimal.
quotes: The most basic type of definitional information is the argument constraint: knowledge of what types of entities can be the values of a predicate or function.
(isa biologicalMother IrreflexiveBinaryPredicate)
(arg2Isa biologicalMother FemaleAnimal)
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the term and give the example.

assertions.value: The authors state that, rather than write a repetitive axiom for each irreflexive predicate, Cyc introduces the collection IrreflexiveBinaryPredicate, puts the logical feature in one axiom that references it, and makes new predicates instances of it.
quotes: the pattern of such an axiom is uselessly repetitive
expressing that logical feature in an axiom that references the collection, and making new predicates instances of the collection
assertions.reader_inference: The text states this as a design strategy; no measure of the saving is given.

assertions.value: The paper gives the CycL definitional axiom for arg1Isa: for all PRED, TYPE, X and VARS, if (arg1Isa PRED TYPE) and (PRED X VARS) hold then (isa X TYPE).
quotes: (forAll ?PRED (forAll ?TYPE (forAll ?X (forAll ?VARS (implies (and (arg1Isa ?PRED ?TYPE) (?PRED ?X ?VARS)) (isa ?X ?TYPE))))))
assertions.certainty_reason: The axiom is stated in the paper.

assertions.value: The paper states that genls is the basic sub-class predicate and the basis of the taxonomic hierarchy, is declared transitive and reflexive, and is defined by the axiom that if (genls TYPE1 TYPE2) and (isa X TYPE1) hold then (isa X TYPE2).
quotes: The predicate genls is the basic sub-class predicate and it is the basis of the taxonomic hierarchy.
(isa genls TransitiveBinaryPredicate) (isa genls ReflexiveBinaryPredicate)
(implies (and (genls ?TYPE1 ?TYPE2) (isa ?X ?TYPE1)) (isa ?X ?TYPE2))
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the definitional assertions and axiom.

assertions.value: The authors state that genls expresses inheritance among types and structures the ontology, while disjointWith states that two collections do not share any members.
quotes: while disjointWith states that two collections do not share any members
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the predicate.

assertions.value: The authors state that comment, the main documentation predicate, has the assertions arg1QuotedIsa CycLIndexedTerm and arg2QuotedIsa SubLString, so its class restrictions apply to the terms themselves and not to the concepts they denote, which keeps ontology-management knowledge inside the ontology.
quotes: (arg1QuotedIsa comment CycLIndexedTerm) (arg2QuotedIsa comment SubLString)
so the class restrictions on the arguments are not relative to the concepts denoted by the terms, but to the terms themselves
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors give the assertions and the explanation.

assertions.value: The authors acknowledge a common criticism that most OpenCyc predicates are not fully populated and lack axiomatizing rules, grant that there is merit to it, and reply that a huge body of such knowledge is encoded in the definitional assertions.
quotes: A common criticism of OpenCyc is that although it includes a large number of predicates, most of those predicates are not fully ‘populated’
Although there is merit to those criticisms, they fail to acknowledge that a huge body of such knowledge is encoded in the definitional assertions
assertions.reader_inference: The reply is an argument by the OpenCyc authors, with no measurement.

assertions.value: The authors claim that taxonomic and definitional constraints are more efficient than ubiquitous axiomatization, and that a strong high-level ontology with inheritance allows a more efficient and thorough expression of common-sense facts than writing a rule.
quotes: Those constraints are more efficient than if they were to be ubiquitously axiomatized.
a strong ontology of high-level knowledge, with inheritance, allows for a more efficient and thorough expression of common sense facts

assertions.value: The authors state that a fundamental distinction in the ontology is between collections and individuals, and that historical knowledge typically concerns individual events, countries and persons, while chemical and other scientific knowledge is typically described by properties of an entire class.
assertions.anchor: Content of the Cyc Ontology, p.3
quotes: One of the fundamental distinctions in the ontology is between collections and individuals.
chemical and other scientific knowledge is typically described in terms of the properties of an entire

assertions.value: The authors state that the upper ontology includes collections of collections, such as ExistingObjectType and ExistingStuffType, whose instances correspond to the count or mass interpretations of nouns.
assertions.anchor: Content of the Cyc Ontology, p.3
quotes: ExistingObjectType and ExistingStuffType are second-order collections whose instances correspond to the count or mass interpretations of nouns
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state what the collections are.

assertions.value: The authors state that the functional expression (SubcollectionOfWithRelationToFn Ambassador basedInRegion Turkey) denotes the collection of all ambassadors to Turkey.
assertions.anchor: Content of the Cyc Ontology, p.3
quotes: (SubcollectionOfWithRelationToFn Ambassador basedInRegion Turkey)
is the collection of all ambassadors to Turkey.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the meaning of the expression.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Cyc KB is traditionally divided into upper, middle and lower ontologies by level of generality; the upper is the smallest but most broadly referenced, the middle is widely used but not universal, and the lower holds domain-specific leaf-level knowledge and is the largest segment but least broadly applicable.
assertions.anchor: Upper, Middle, and Lower Cyc Ontology, p.3
quotes: The Cyc KB is traditionally subdivided into the upper, middle, and lower ontologies.
is the smallest but most broadly referenced area of the Cyc ontology
This layer accounts for the largest segment of knowledge in the KB, but the least broadly applicable.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the three layers.

assertions.value: The paper states that Event is a specialization of Situation and that each instance of Event is a dynamic situation in which the state of the world changes, and that Events should not be confused with TimeIntervals.
quotes: Each instance of Event is a dynamic situation in which the state of the world changes
Events should not be confused with TimeIntervals.
assertions.certainty_reason: The comment assertion defines the term.

assertions.value: The paper lists assertions for Event including (genls Event Situation), (disjointWith Event PositiveDimensionalThing) and (genls HelicopterLanding Event), and marks the last as inferred knowledge.
quotes: (genls Event Situation)
(disjointWith Event PositiveDimensionalThing)
(genls HelicopterLanding Event) inferred knowledge
assertions.certainty_reason: The assertions are listed in the paper.

assertions.value: The paper states a rule that if an agent causes a Situation in some sense, the agent plays the role of causal actor, and a rule that if a situation provides a motive for an agent to play a role in a kind of event, the likelihood of that event increases.
quotes: If there is a situation that is caused (in some sense) by some agent, that agent plays the role of causal actor.
the likelihood of that event occurring increases
assertions.certainty_reason: The rules are given as example assertions in the paper.

assertions.value: The paper gives SocialGathering as a middle-ontology example: a specialization of SocialOccurrence with communication between participants, so that a group waiting to board an elevator is not typically a SocialGathering, with required actor slot attendees and a suggested dateOfEvent.
quotes: Note that a group of people waiting to board an elevator is not typically a SocialGathering
(requiredActorSlots SocialGathering attendees)
Although it is not semantically required, it is likely that getting a dateOfEvent assertion
assertions.certainty_reason: The assertions define the term in the paper.

assertions.value: The paper gives ChemicalReaction as a lower-ontology example: a subcollection of PhysicalTransformationEvent in which two or more substances undergo chemical change, with subcollections including CombustionReaction, ExothermicReaction and Fermenting, and a strong suggestion that a catalyst be given.
quotes: Each instance of ChemicalReaction is an event in which two or more substances undergo a chemical change
(genls ExothermicReaction ChemicalReaction)
(keGenlsStrongSuggestionPreds-RelationAllExists ChemicalReaction catalyst)
assertions.certainty_reason: The assertions define the term in the paper.

assertions.value: The paper gives the catalyst predicate: (catalyst R X) means ChemicalReaction R has the quantity of substance X as a catalyst; arg1Isa is ChemicalReaction, arg2Isa is PartiallyTangible, and enzymes are capable of being catalysts in chemical reactions.
quotes: (catalyst R X) means that the ChemicalReaction R has the particular quantity of substance X as a catalyst.
(arg1Isa catalyst ChemicalReaction)
Enzymes are capable of being catalysts in chemical reactions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The assertions define the predicate in the paper.

assertions.value: The paper states that each instance of CombustionReaction is a rapid chemical reaction that produces a flame, with outputsCreated-TypeType CombustionReaction Flame.
quotes: Each instance of CombustionReaction is a rapid chemical reaction that produces a flame.
assertions.certainty_reason: The comment assertion defines the term.

assertions.value: The paper presents a partial CycL representation of Martin Luther burning a papal bull in Wittenburg on 10 December 1520 as a test that the KB can describe a novel event, using preexisting terms, with BurningOfPapalBull as a SocialGathering and at least forty university students attending.
quotes: The true test of the significance of repository of knowledge is whether it can be used to describe a novel event
(dateOfEvent BurningOfPapalBull (DayFn 10 (MonthFn December (YearFn 1520))))
At least forty university students attended the event.
assertions.reader_inference: One worked example, with no evaluation on other events or by other users.

assertions.value: The authors state that the distinction between the conceptual work and the specific copy burned prevents Cyc from concluding that the conceptual work has been utterly destroyed, in the same way that burning a copy of Moby Dick does not destroy the work.
quotes: The distinction between the conceptual artifact and the specific copy being burned prevents Cyc from concluding that the conceptual work has been utterly destroyed

assertions.value: The authors state that the sub-event that caused the burning is defined implicitly with a thereExists, unlike the reified social gathering and burning events, because there is nothing else to say about it.
quotes: this event is defined implicitly, because there is nothing else to say about it

assertions.value: The authors report that OpenCyc has supported research ranging from automatic pruning of irrelevant knowledge, to integration of Semantic Web metadata, to obtaining part of speech information from natural language data by machine learning.
quotes: OpenCyc has been used to support research in areas ranging from automatic pruning of irrelevant knowledge
assertions.reader_inference: The uses are cited to other papers, not examined here.

assertions.value: The authors state that OpenCyc has been criticized for being restrictive, particularly for instance-level knowledge, for lacking any reasoning capability, and for being formally inconsistent, and that the last is difficult to overcome in a very large, largely hand-tooled knowledge base.
quotes: The OpenCyc system has been criticized for being restrictive, particularly with respect to instance-level knowledge, for lacking any reasoning capability, and being formally inconsistent.
While the last is difficult to overcome in a very large, largely hand-tooled knowledge base
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limits and concede inconsistency.

assertions.value: The authors state that the release of ResearchCyc, available without charge for research use, at least partially addresses concerns about coverage, and that it includes extensive instance-level population.
quotes: have been at least partially addressed by the release of ResearchCyc
extensive instance-level population

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the work produced an extensive taxonomy of concepts and terms and a large self-reflective vocabulary for describing common definitional needs, and they invite other researchers to use ResearchCyc and OpenCyc.
quotes: we have developed both an extensive taxonomy of concepts and terms, and a large, selfreflective vocabulary for describing the most common definitional needs
We invite other researchers to make use of the ResearchCyc and OpenCyc platforms

assertions.value: The paper reports no experiment, benchmark or quantitative evaluation of Cyc's reasoning or coverage; its evidence is descriptive examples and size counts.
quotes: The terms mentioned are intended as examples of the taxonomic knowledge available in OpenCyc
assertions.reader_inference: Inferred from the whole text; the paper states no such limit itself.
